events.text: Your cloud-barge and another meet at the narrow turn of the Sea of Clouds, and neither pilot will give way. The other barge's passenger, {npc}, leans over the rail and says the sky is wide enough for two, if one of you stops being proud.
events.arc: The Narrow Turn of the Cloud-Road

choices.text: Give way with a bow

mem.note: gave way to me on the cloud-road

effects.log: Your barge drifts aside. {npc} laughs, bows back, and drops a pressed cloud-blossom on your deck.

choices.text: Hold the lane and offer a race to the next isle

mem.note: raced me across the clouds

effects.log: "A race, then," says {npc}, and the two pilots curse as one. The cloud-wind sings in your sails.

choices.text: Offer to tow them through the turn

effects.log: You throw a line across. {npc} catches it, grinning, and the two barges swing through together like one animal.

events.text: You meet {npc} again at a mooring-post on the Floating Isles, by chance or by someone's arrangement. {He} has kept the cloud-blossom and tucked it into a sleeve. The mooring-keeper pretends to count rope and listens with both ears.
events.arc: The Narrow Turn of the Cloud-Road

choices.text: Ask what {he} does with the flower

mem.note: kept the blossom I gave

effects.log: "I press things I want to remember," {npc} says, and then, caught, looks at the water.

choices.text: Invite {him} to ride the long way to the Jade Court

effects.log: The long way takes nine days. Neither of you mentions that the short way takes two.

choices.text: Stay quiet and watch the clouds with {him}

effects.log: You watch the clouds change colour. It is the most you have said to anyone in years.

events.text: Nine days on one barge, and {npc} has learned the way you steer and you have learned the way {he} hums. At the Jade Court quay, {he} must go one way and you the other. The pilot politely turns {his} back.
events.arc: The Narrow Turn of the Cloud-Road

choices.text: Ask {npc} to take the road beside you

mem.note: asked me to share the road

effects.log: {npc} says yes before you finish the sentence, then pretends the barge needed steering.

choices.text: Give {him} the barge-pennant to remember you by

mem.note: gave me a pennant

effects.log: The pennant goes into {his} sleeve beside the flower. It is not a promise, but it is close.

events.text: The race ends at the third isle, and you lose by a hand's breadth, and {npc} does not gloat. {He} sits on the dock with wet sleeves and asks if you always race when you like someone, or only when it is hopeless.
events.arc: The Narrow Turn of the Cloud-Road

choices.text: Admit it is both

mem.note: won a year of my company

effects.log: You admit it, to the dock and the water and {him}. {npc} says the prize for winning is your company for a year.

choices.text: Say you only race for the view

effects.log: "Then take the view," says {npc}, and rides off. You are not sure which of you lost.

events.text: At the Jade Court's morning audience the seating is assigned by the Rolls, and a clerk of the Lotus Ledger places you beside {npc}, an immortal of a rival branch. The Keeper's brush hovers over both your names, and the clerk looks apologetic.
events.arc: A Seat Beside the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Greet {npc} formally and trade court gossip

mem.note: shared court gossip on the first day

effects.log: You trade three useful rumours. {npc} gives one back, and it is better than yours.

choices.text: Ask the clerk what the Ledger says about the two of you

effects.log: The clerk goes pale and says the Ledger is not to be read aloud. {npc} bursts out laughing.

choices.text: Sit silently and let the audience pass

effects.log: You sit like jade through three hours of petitions. {npc} admires it. So does the Keeper.

events.text: A petition comes up that touches both your branches, and for a month you and {npc} are bound to draft a joint reply. It is dull work, ink and seals, but {he} turns every clause into a small joke and your hand goes steadier by the day.
events.arc: A Seat Beside the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Take the harder clauses and let {him} finish the rest

mem.note: split the petition with me

effects.log: You take the thorny clauses. {npc} cuts the draft by half. The reply is praised.

choices.text: Put your own seal beside {his}

mem.note: sealed beside me before all the Court

effects.log: Two seals on one page is a quiet scandal at the Court. The Keeper notes it in a smaller hand.

events.text: The Keeper of the Lotus Ledger calls you both aside. The Rolls, the Keeper says, have a gap where a union would fit, and the Court likes gaps filled. {npc} says nothing, and looks at you rather than at the Keeper.
events.arc: A Seat Beside the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Ask {npc} to wed, and let the Rolls follow

mem.note: proposed before the Keeper

effects.log: The Keeper writes it down before you finish. {npc} says the proposal was neat enough to hang.

choices.text: Decline the Court's nudge, and court {him} in private

mem.note: chose me over the Rolls

effects.log: The Keeper puts the brush down. {npc} says yes to the private way and no to the Rolls, for now.

events.text: Two seals on one page are noticed. A House elder sends word that the Court expects an announcement, and {npc} meets you in a corridor of white jade, quiet. "We can make it plain, or make it grand," {he} says. "I would like it plain."
events.arc: A Seat Beside the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Make it plain: a cup of tea before the Keeper

mem.note: chose a plain wedding with me

effects.log: You take tea in the Keeper's office, two cups and a short scroll. It is the happiest hour of your year.

choices.text: Make it grand, to quiet the elders

mem.note: agreed to a grand wedding for the elders' sake

effects.log: Grand it is: a hundred banners and every House at the table. {npc} bears it with a fixed smile and a hand clasped tight in yours.

events.text: {npc} is your friend of two decades when Lord Seol Gahan of the House of the Frost Moon arrives with a hundred pearls and a letter of proposal in perfect calligraphy. The pearls are not for you. The Lord is courting {npc}, and {npc} looks at you across the hall.
events.arc: The Suitor of the Frost Moon

choices.text: Wish the Lord well and say nothing

mem.note: let a rival suitor come unopposed

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} drops {his} eyes. The Lord is charming, and that is the worst of it.

choices.text: Offer the Lord a game of stones for the right to speak

effects.log: Stones on a jade board are an old way to settle a courtship. The Lord accepts with a bow.

choices.text: Take {npc} aside and ask what {he} wants

mem.note: asked me what I wanted

effects.log: {npc} wants to be asked, it seems, before being given. You have not yet asked.

events.text: Lord Seol is better than you hoped: well-read, kind to servants, a poet of the frost. {npc} spends the autumn in the Lord's company and returns each time a little more confused. The Lord, to be fair, never speaks ill of you.
events.arc: The Suitor of the Frost Moon

choices.text: Ask {npc} to choose by their own heart

mem.note: would not compete dishonestly

effects.log: You say you will not compete, only be honest. {npc} is quiet, and then holds your sleeve a moment too long.

choices.text: Enter the field openly: a poem in the Lord's own style

mem.note: wrote me a rival poem

effects.log: The poem is not bad. The Lord reads it twice and says, graciously, that verse has met its match.

events.text: On the night of the Frost Moon feast, the Lord asks for your leave to speak with {npc} on the terrace, and you give it. When {npc} returns, {he} is smiling, and takes your hand before the whole hall. The Lord bows from across the room.
events.arc: The Suitor of the Frost Moon

choices.text: Take the hand and thank the Lord with a cup

mem.note: chose me over the Frost Moon

effects.log: You raise a cup to the Lord. Lord Seol says that the House of the Frost Moon loses a bride and gains a friend.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to wed, right there, in the lamps

mem.note: said yes before the Frost Moon feast

effects.log: The hall holds its breath. {npc} says yes, and the Lord leads the applause, a shade too hard.

events.text: The game of stones ends in a draw, and the Lord, to everyone's surprise, laughs and says a draw means the lady decides. {npc} decides in a month, and not the Lord. The Frost Moon takes it with grace and sends a gift of silver tea the next year.
events.arc: The Suitor of the Frost Moon

choices.text: Accept the choice quietly and send the Lord a thank-you scroll

mem.note: was chosen over a better suitor, and was kind about it

effects.log: The scroll is short and warm. The Lord, they say, framed it.

choices.text: Take {npc} to see the Frost Moon rise from the White Stairs

mem.note: climbed the stairs with me for the moon

effects.log: The stairs are cold and the moon enormous. {npc} leans on your shoulder the whole way down.

events.text: A crane lands in your courtyard with a letter tied to its leg, from {npc}, whom you met once at a banquet. The crane-post between the far isles takes years: the date on the paper is a decade old, and the writer has surely forgotten what was asked.
events.arc: A Letter Ten Years in Flight

choices.text: Write back that very hour

mem.note: wrote back the same hour

effects.log: Your reply goes out on the same crane, which looks offended. The ink is still wet when it clears the roof.

choices.text: Wait a season before answering, to find the right words

effects.log: It takes you a whole season. You discard nine drafts. The tenth is shorter than any of them.

choices.text: Send a pressed cloud-blossom instead of words

mem.note: sent me a flower and no words

effects.log: The crane takes it, puzzled. A blossom takes a decade to say what ten pages might.

events.text: Another letter arrives, from the same hand, and this one answers something you did not write. You have been replying to different versions of each other for years, and by the time the cranes cross, you both have changed.
events.arc: A Letter Ten Years in Flight

choices.text: Write plainly about who you are now

mem.note: told me who they truly were

effects.log: You describe the person who actually reads the letters: tired, hopeful, a little cruel before breakfast. It feels like confession.

choices.text: Keep writing to the person in the old letters

effects.log: You keep the old tone, a courtesy and a cage. {npc} will meet someone else at the end of the road.

events.text: Eighteen years after the first letter, {npc} lands on your terrace, tired, windblown, holding the last of your replies. "I came in person," {he} says, "because the cranes could not carry the rest of what I wanted to say."
events.arc: A Letter Ten Years in Flight

choices.text: Take {npc} inside and say the rest back

mem.note: crossed the isles in person after a decade of letters

effects.log: You say the rest back, all at once. It takes an hour, and a pot of tea gone cold.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to stay a season and see

mem.note: stayed a season to see if it was real

effects.log: A season becomes three. {npc} says the isles seem closer when one has a reason.

events.text: {npc} comes, but the person who steps off the cloud-barge is not the one in the letters. "I am sorry," {he} says. "I changed. So did you." You sit together in silence, two strangers who know each other's handwriting better than their faces.
events.arc: A Letter Ten Years in Flight

choices.text: Start again from the beginning, as strangers

mem.note: started again with me after the letters

effects.log: You start again. It is slow and a little sad, and then, after a month, it is not sad at all.

choices.text: Thank {him} for the letters and let it rest

mem.note: was thanked and let go

effects.log: You thank {him}. You keep the whole box of letters until it is dust. {npc} leaves on the next barge, still kind.

events.text: In the second year of the Isle War you meet {npc} across a truce-table, an envoy of the opposing power. The terms are cold. Over the tea afterward {he} remarks on the light through the window, and you realise the first thing you noticed was the way {he} said it.
events.arc: Courting Across the War of the Five Powers

choices.text: Reply with an honest remark about the light

mem.note: spoke truly at the truce-table

effects.log: You reply. It is the first true sentence either of you has spoken at that table in a month.

choices.text: Keep to terms and write down {his} name

effects.log: You write {his} name in your ledger of the other side. It sits there, oddly, between treaties.

choices.text: Slip a note under the teacup

mem.note: slipped me a note under a teacup

effects.log: The note says only that the tea was good. {npc} does not look up, but the cup is carried away carefully.

events.text: The truce collapses. {npc}'s barges and yours fire on each other over the Sea of Clouds. For a season you send no word, and then a crane arrives with a sprig of cloud-fern: a code you once joked about at the truce-table, which means "I am alive."
events.arc: Courting Across the War of the Five Powers

choices.text: Send the fern back, doubled

mem.note: answered the fern in the middle of the war

effects.log: Two fern fronds means "so am I." You send the answer by a neutral boatman who asks no questions.

choices.text: Burn the fern and report the contact

mem.note: burned my fern and gave me up

effects.log: The fern burns green. You report a leak in your own lines. Nobody asks who sent it.

events.text: The war ends in a peace neither side likes. At the signing, {npc} stands among the other side's delegates, and when the seals are pressed, {he} looks at you and holds up two sprigs of cloud-fern, tied together with red thread.
events.arc: Courting Across the War of the Five Powers

choices.text: Cross the hall and take the thread

mem.note: crossed a hall of enemies for me

effects.log: You cross the hall in front of both delegations. Somebody coughs. {npc} ties the thread round your wrist before the peace is dry.

choices.text: Arrange to meet by the cloud-gap at dusk

mem.note: met me by the gap after the war

effects.log: There are no delegations at the gap, only two people and a lot to say. {npc} says the war was a bad way to meet.

events.text: After the peace, {npc} comes to you in the dusk, not as a lover but as a witness. "You gave me up," {he} says. "You were right, by your lights. I came to see whether you would look at me while I said it." The corridor is long and empty.
events.arc: Courting Across the War of the Five Powers

choices.text: Look at {him} and say you would do it again

mem.note: looked at me and said they would do it again

effects.log: You say it plainly. {npc} nods, and walks out, and for years there is only a faint scent of fern in the corridor.

choices.text: Ask {him} to hate you properly, if it helps

mem.note: let me hate them until I could stop

effects.log: "It helps," says {npc}, and for an hour hates you with real skill. Then {he} laughs, shakily, and sits down.

events.text: The Red Thread Elder of the Jade Court, a small grey immortal named Mu Haeng, arrives at your grotto uninvited and unrolls a scroll of matches. One name is circled in red: {npc}. "The Court needs you two paired," Mu Haeng says, "for reasons I am not at liberty to share."

choices.text: Refuse the match on principle

mem.note: refused the Elder's match

effects.log: The Elder sighs, rolls the scroll, and says refusal is common and rarely lasts.

choices.text: Ask to meet {npc} before you decide

effects.log: "A sensible request," says the Elder. "Meet at the Pavilion of Quiet Tea. I shall not attend." The Elder attends.

choices.text: Ask why the Court wants it

effects.log: The Elder's reasons turn out to be tangled and small, a border dispute and a sulking House. You laugh, and the Elder, to your surprise, laughs too.

events.text: {npc} turns out to be more reasonable than the scroll. At the Pavilion of Quiet Tea you both agree, in the first quarter-hour, that the Elder is meddling. The second quarter-hour, you discover you agree on a great deal more. The Elder, hiding behind a screen, is delighted.

choices.text: Admit the match may not be a mistake

mem.note: admitted the match might not be a mistake

effects.log: You say so. The screen shakes with a restrained cough, and {npc} hides a smile in a teacup.

choices.text: Insist on courting {him} the ordinary way

mem.note: insisted on courting me the ordinary way

effects.log: You insist on the ordinary way. {npc} says the ordinary way sounds like a lot of walking. It is.

events.text: A year of the ordinary way, and the Red Thread Elder keeps turning up in your gardens with a face of innocent coincidence. At last {npc} takes Mu Haeng by the sleeve. "We are going to marry," {he} says. "You may stop pretending to be a bush."

choices.text: Thank the Elder, and send a good jar of wine to the Elder's door

mem.note: married me despite the Elder's meddling

effects.log: The Elder weeps into the wine and claims it is the steam. It is a good wine.

choices.text: Tell the Elder the credit is entirely theirs

mem.note: gave the Elder the credit

effects.log: Mu Haeng pretends great surprise and writes it in the Rolls in beautiful brush: matched by the Elder. You do not argue.

events.text: The Elder's scroll is still in your drawer, with the red circle. {npc} has never once asked about it. At last you tell {him} there was a match, and the Court wanted it. "I know," says {npc}. "I was told too. I came because I wanted to, and kept coming to prove it."

choices.text: Burn the scroll together

mem.note: burned the Elder's scroll with me

effects.log: The scroll burns pink, red, then a lovely grey. There is nothing left of the Court's plan but ash and the two of you.

choices.text: Keep the scroll as a joke between you

mem.note: made the Elder's meddling our joke

effects.log: It lives in a drawer for centuries, taken out for anniversaries. It never once stops being funny.

events.text: {npc} has been your friend for sixty years, a blink at your age, and tonight on the observatory roof {he} says something that takes you a full minute to hear. "I think I have been in love with you for a little while," {he} says. "A decade or so. I wanted to be sure."

choices.text: Say you need time

mem.note: gave me all the time I needed

effects.log: "Take it," says {npc}, serene. "I have time. It is the one thing we have." And {he} means it.

choices.text: Say you felt it too, and did not dare

mem.note: was loved patiently, for a decade

effects.log: You say so, haltingly. {npc} does not move for a long moment. Then the stars come out one by one.

events.text: A century passes the way a century does up here: a long afternoon. You and {npc} write, and meet, and quarrel about nothing, and one day you realise it has been love all along. {He} brings you a small jade box. Inside is a single snow-plum seed.

choices.text: Plant it together on the observatory roof

mem.note: planted a plum seed to wait for

effects.log: The plum seed takes a hundred years to bloom. You plan, quietly, to be there.

choices.text: Say you do not need a century to be sure

mem.note: said they did not need a century

effects.log: Your own certainty startles you. {npc} says, wondering, that you were never slow, only unhurried.

events.text: The plum blooms, a hundred and twelve years after it was planted. {npc} stands beside the flowering branch in a robe the colour of snow. "Now," {he} says, "I am sure. May I finally ask?" The petals fall on the roof like a very small, very slow storm.

choices.text: Say yes before {he} finishes the question

mem.note: asked after a hundred years and a plum tree

effects.log: You say yes so fast that {npc} laughs. A hundred years, and it ends in a laugh.

choices.text: Ask {him} first, to be fair

mem.note: was asked by me first, after all that time

effects.log: You ask. {npc} says that is the first time you have ever been faster than a century, and says yes.

events.text: {npc} proposes to you at last, in the observatory on the night of a rare conjunction, and you realise you have already accepted without noticing, thirty years ago, over soup. Neither of you remembers saying so. It seems that is how it was done.

choices.text: Make it official, a decade late

mem.note: had already accepted over soup

effects.log: You have the Keeper write it down. The Keeper says there is a note already: "Settled, soup."

choices.text: Stay unofficial, and keep being surprised

mem.note: stayed unofficial and in love

effects.log: You stay unofficial for another century, a cheerful scandal at the Court. Nobody minds. Your tea is always warm.

events.text: At the Pavilion of Falling Stars {npc}, a junior stargazer, misreads an omen and sends the whole pavilion into a panic. You are the one who corrects the chart, and for that, {npc} owes you a debt. {He} promises to repay it, with great ceremony, in a year.

choices.text: Say there is no debt

mem.note: tried to forgive a debt that I kept

effects.log: "There is," says {npc}. "I will find it a place to live." The pavilion has a new running joke.

choices.text: Name a price in star-tea

effects.log: "Star-tea," says {npc}, writing it in a notebook. A promise has been struck at the Pavilion of Falling Stars.

events.text: A year later, {npc} turns up at your door with a box of star-tea and an enormous apology: the debt was paid, then miscounted, then paid again. Now {he} is in credit to the tune of six boxes. The two of you sit and drink them, and count stars from your terrace.

choices.text: Count stars until the tea runs out

mem.note: counted stars with me over six boxes of tea

effects.log: You count three hundred and nine. {npc} claims to have counted three hundred and twelve, and the argument is the best of the year.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read your star-chart

mem.note: read my chart and blushed

effects.log: The chart reads strangely: a cross-over, a meeting. {npc} blushes and does not say what it says.

events.text: The Pavilion elders ask you to be the witness at {npc}'s star-casting, the ceremony that proves a stargazer worthy. When the time comes {npc} reads the omen aloud, plain: "The star over this witness is the star over me." The elders raise their eyebrows.

choices.text: Accept the omen openly

mem.note: read my star and yours as one

effects.log: You say that you saw it too. The pavilion applauds, politely. {npc} is already weeping, quietly, into a sleeve.

choices.text: Ask for a year before you answer the sky

mem.note: asked a year to answer the omen

effects.log: The sky can wait a year, and does. {npc} agrees without sulking. The stars, in due time, agree too.

events.text: The chart {npc} read for you hangs in the Pavilion, and visitors stop and look at it, and whisper. {He} finds you on the terrace and offers to burn it, if you are embarrassed. "But I should say," {he} adds, "I think it is correct."

choices.text: Ask {him} to leave it hanging

mem.note: hung our chart for the world to see

effects.log: "Hanging it stays," says {npc}. And you both stand under it, and say nothing, and everything is quite clear.

choices.text: Propose, to make the chart true

mem.note: made our chart come true

effects.log: The chart, they say, was true already. {npc} says yes and uses the word "obviously" four times.

events.text: A clerk of the Lotus Ledger tracks you down, mortified. A century ago, an error entered the Rolls: your name was written beside {npc}'s as a spouse, though you had never met. The Rolls, by custom, are never wrong. The Keeper wants an answer by the next court.
events.arc: The Error in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Demand the error be struck

mem.note: agreed it was an error

effects.log: The clerk reports to the Keeper, who sighs. {npc}, hearing of it, writes you a very dry note offering to share the correction fee.

choices.text: Go and meet {npc} first

mem.note: met me because of a clerk's mistake

effects.log: {npc} lives in a quiet grotto, and is, you discover, as bewildered as you. You share tea over the Ledger's clerical error.

events.text: The Keeper says the Rolls can be corrected only if both parties declare a lack of affection under the Lotus Seal. You and {npc} must each go to the Seal Hall and say, aloud, that you do not love the other. Neither of you has met the other for more than a week.
events.arc: The Error in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Go to the Seal Hall and say the words

mem.note: said the words in the Seal Hall

effects.log: The words come out easily. The Seal flickers and holds a moment longer than it should. {npc} watches from the door, pensive.

choices.text: Postpone the declaration, to know {him} better

mem.note: asked for a year before the Seal

effects.log: The Keeper grants a year. In that year you learn what {npc} puts in tea and what {he} is afraid of at night.

events.text: The year ends. In the Seal Hall the Keeper holds out a brush, and {npc} takes it, and your heart does something it did not do at the Jade Banquet. {He} writes, in a slow hand, a different sentence. Under the Lotus Seal it reads: "I accept the error."
events.arc: The Error in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Add your own name beneath

mem.note: accepted the Ledger's error with me

effects.log: The Seal glows white and settles. The Keeper blinks and observes this is the first time in three thousand years the Rolls have been right by accident.

choices.text: Hold the brush and ask for another year

mem.note: asked for another year with me

effects.log: "The Rolls are patient," says the Keeper. "They have to be."

events.text: You both say the words, and the Seal does not flicker. The Keeper strikes the line. For a moment nothing happens. Then {npc} laughs, as if freed, and asks what you would like for supper. You walk to a noodle stall together, relieved, and ordinary.
events.arc: The Error in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Share a noodle bowl and be friends

mem.note: became my friend after the Rolls were corrected

effects.log: You become friends, surprisingly easily. Neither of you ever forgets the clerk's apology, framed on your wall.

choices.text: Keep meeting for noodles, and see

mem.note: kept meeting me after the Rolls were corrected

effects.log: You keep meeting for noodles. It is not love, not yet, but it is the sort of friendship love might be born from.

events.text: You are halfway up the White Stairs when you overtake {npc}, a newly ascending immortal resting on a landing with the shaky face of someone who has climbed for a thousand steps and been told it is a thousand more. The stair does not allow a hand to be lent.

choices.text: Sit beside {him} for a while

mem.note: sat with me on the White Stairs

effects.log: You sit and share water. {npc} says nobody has sat beside them in a long time. The stair hums.

choices.text: Walk slowly alongside, not helping

mem.note: matched my pace on the stairs

effects.log: Hands cannot help on the stair, but company may. {npc} sets a rhythm; you match it.

events.text: The stair tests {npc} at the thousandth step with a vision of everyone left behind below. {He} stops, trembling, and you stand at the same step, seeing your own. Neither can climb on until the other says something true about what they left.

choices.text: Speak first: say what you left below

mem.note: spoke first on the thousandth step

effects.log: You say it aloud, a mother's voice at a window. The vision loosens. {npc} says a name in return.

choices.text: Wait for {him} to speak, and listen

mem.note: listened to what I left below

effects.log: {npc} speaks for a long time. You listen to every word, and the vision lets go of you both.

events.text: At the top the Jade Court's Gate opens, one person at a time. {npc} offers you the first place; you offer {him} the first place. A gatekeeper clears their throat. Both of you laugh, and the gate decides for you by opening for a double-width entry.

choices.text: Walk through together, hand in hand

mem.note: passed through the Gate with me

effects.log: The gate lets you both through at once, an honour it has not given in six hundred years. {npc} grips your hand.

choices.text: Walk through side by side, hands to yourselves

mem.note: walked beside me through the Gate

effects.log: Side by side but not touching, as the stair's code demands. It is not the same, but nearly, and you smile at each other through the Gate.

events.text: At the top, {npc} goes through the Gate first, while you are still catching your breath at the final landing. They wait for you inside, on a jade bench. "I was afraid you would leave me on the stair," {he} says. "You do not strike me as someone who would. But I was afraid."

choices.text: Tell {him} you never would

mem.note: told me they would never leave me on the stair

effects.log: "I know," says {npc}. "I am still glad to hear it." The bench is wide, and you sit on it.

choices.text: Tell {him} you nearly did

mem.note: confessed they nearly left me behind

effects.log: You tell the truth. {npc} considers, and says that honesty on the thousandth step is worth a thousand kindnesses.

events.text: The House of the Silent Bell keeps a vow of silence for the first century of each member's life, and {npc} has just broken it. At a banquet you hear a voice you have never heard, rusty and low, say your name. The hall turns to look.
events.arc: The House of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Reply softly and sit beside {him}

mem.note: spoke to me first when I broke silence

effects.log: You sit. {npc} says seven words and is exhausted. You get {him} some water, and the hall resumes its murmur.

choices.text: Ask why {he} chose to break the vow now

mem.note: broke a century of silence for me

effects.log: "For you," says {npc}, and the hall goes very quiet again.

events.text: The House elders are displeased. {npc} is summoned to the Hall of the Bell, and you are not allowed in. You wait outside under a great silent bell with a clapper bound in white silk. Hours later, {npc} walks out, hoarse, and says, "I am still permitted to speak."
events.arc: The House of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Ask what it cost

mem.note: offered to pay half the cost of my voice

effects.log: "A tenth of the House's regard," says {npc}. "A fair price." You offer to pay half of it in whatever way you can.

choices.text: Offer a peace-gift to the House elders

mem.note: made peace with my House for me

effects.log: A gift of silk and silver tea soothes the elders. {npc} watches your face with growing wonder.

events.text: On the anniversary of the broken vow, the Silent Bell is struck, the first time in a thousand years. Its voice is low and full and everyone in the House weeps without knowing why. {npc} takes your hand and says, "I think I am allowed to say it now."
events.arc: The House of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Hear it out and answer with the same words

mem.note: said the same words back to me beneath the Bell

effects.log: You say the same words back. The Bell rings once, softly, as if approving.

choices.text: Say it needs no words, and pour tea

mem.note: answered me in silence and tea

effects.log: You pour tea in silence. {npc} understands, and laughs, and says that silence can also be a promise.

events.text: The Silent Bell's House makes you an offer: marry into the line, and keep the vow of silence for ten years, as a courtesy. {npc} looks at you and does not say that it is unfair. You can see that they very much wish you would say yes anyway.
events.arc: The House of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Agree to the silent decade

mem.note: kept a decade of silence for me

effects.log: Ten years of silence, and the gestures you invent in them become your private language for life.

choices.text: Refuse the silence, and ask them to leave the House

mem.note: left the Silent Bell for me

effects.log: "I will," says {npc}. "I was always going to, if you asked." The House sends you a bell the size of a thimble.

events.text: The House of the Thunder Gate has chosen {npc} for you. The Elders brought the proposal with three attendants, a dowry of lightning-glass, and a ledger of mutual benefits. {npc} was not asked either, and says so, quite loudly, from the doorway.

choices.text: Refuse politely, citing a prior commitment

mem.note: refused our arranged match with courtesy

effects.log: You cite the prior commitment of being unmarried and happy. The Elders' faces tighten. {npc} hides a laugh behind a sleeve.

choices.text: Agree to meet, on neutral ground

mem.note: met me in disguise to escape the match

effects.log: You agree to a meeting at a roadside tea-house. {npc} turns up in disguise as a waiter.

events.text: Whether or not you refuse, the Thunder Gate is not deterred. A hundred lightning-lanterns appear at your window each night, spelling out proposals in blue sparks. {npc} sends a note: "Sorry about the lanterns. They are my uncle. Possibly I can stop the old man."

choices.text: Write back and ask for a truce

mem.note: negotiated a truce with my uncle's lanterns

effects.log: The truce lasts a month. The lanterns spell out a poem instead, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Visit the House and speak to the Elders directly

mem.note: stood before my House for me

effects.log: You walk into the Thunder Gate Hall alone. The Elders offer you tea, and {npc} is hiding behind the third pillar, beaming.

events.text: The Elders yield, grumbling. The House agrees to a courtship of five years, entirely at your own pace, with no lanterns. At the end of the first year {npc} is waiting in your courtyard with a single quiet lightning-spark in a jar. "My own," {he} says. "Not the House's."

choices.text: Accept the spark and the courtship

mem.note: gave me a private spark

effects.log: You accept. The spark lives on your windowsill, and flickers when {npc} walks past.

choices.text: Propose that you skip the five years

mem.note: skipped five years of courtship with me

effects.log: The Elders object, and then, seeing their own nephew's face, relent. The lightning-glass dowry arrives in a wagon.

events.text: You and {npc} have arranged a tidy friendship, the Elders' lanterns long since retired. At the end of the year, {he} says: "If it were not for them, I would not have met you. Is that not dreadful? I almost have to thank my uncle."

choices.text: Thank the uncle, in verse

mem.note: thanked my uncle for me, badly

effects.log: The uncle receives a very bad poem and, as a result, ceases the lanterns for a century.

choices.text: Say you would have found each other eventually

mem.note: said we would have found each other

effects.log: "Perhaps," says {npc}, "but it would have taken the better part of a thousand years." You do not argue.

events.text: At the Vermilion Phoenix House's yearly feast the custom is that every guest brings a dish of their own making. You bring a modest dumpling. {npc}, a child of the House, tastes it, gasps, and demands to know the recipe in front of the entire table.

choices.text: Share the recipe loudly

mem.note: shared a dumpling recipe in front of everyone

effects.log: You recite the recipe to a hundred guests. The cooks of the House stare, mutinous. {npc} writes it on a napkin.

choices.text: Offer to cook it for {him} alone

mem.note: cooked a dumpling only for me

effects.log: "For me alone?" says {npc}, delighted. The table titters. You realise what you have said.

events.text: A phoenix feast comes with phoenix fire: the House cooks over a flame that does not burn what it should not. {npc} invites you into the kitchens to learn the heat. It is dangerous and absurd, and {he} stands too close, adjusting your hands on the pan.

choices.text: Learn the fire-craft properly

mem.note: taught me the phoenix fire

effects.log: You burn two pans and learn to read the flame by colour. {npc} laughs the whole time, kindly.

choices.text: Pretend to be hopeless to keep {him} close

mem.note: pretended to be hopeless

effects.log: "You are lying," says {npc} presently. "Your wrist is perfect. But I'll allow it."

events.text: At the winter feast, the head of the House calls a toast to the guest who has "brought something new to the table." It is you. {npc} stands, and says that, if it pleases the House, the guest might bring something new to the House itself.

choices.text: Take the cup and answer the toast

mem.note: was toasted by the House with me

effects.log: You drink. The House cheers. {npc} turns pink as a persimmon, and you ask the head for permission in the old words.

choices.text: Ask for time and a phoenix-feather as a pledge

mem.note: pledged me a phoenix feather

effects.log: The head sends a vermilion feather the colour of a lantern. You wear it on your belt for a year.

events.text: The kitchens know. The cooks leave out two extra cups. By the time you and {npc} finally admit that the cooking lessons are an excuse, a whole house of cooks have been keeping a quiet tally on the date. They split a jar of plum wine on the night you speak.

choices.text: Admit it, with flour on your sleeve

mem.note: admitted it in the kitchen with flour in my hair

effects.log: You admit it, floured to the elbow. The cooks sing the House's old wedding song, off-key.

choices.text: Cook a feast for the whole kitchen as thanks

mem.note: fed my whole kitchen in thanks

effects.log: Your feast is a modest triumph. The cooks weep. {npc} says the way to the House is, obviously, through the kitchen.

events.text: The Cloud-Weaver House spins cloud into cloth, and {npc}, one of its youngest weavers, has made a scarf of dawn-cloud for you after a kindness you barely remember. It will fade by midday unless it is cared for properly. {He} explains this with trembling hands.

choices.text: Wear it all morning and keep it alive

mem.note: kept my scarf alive all day

effects.log: You tend the scarf with patient fingers. It lasts until sunset, and {npc} watches it fade with something like wonder.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the care

mem.note: asked me to teach them the weaving

effects.log: The care is a hundred small gestures. {npc} guides your wrists. The scarf glows brighter than it has any right to.

events.text: The Cloud-Weaver House hosts its annual Loom Night, when guests are allowed to try the lesser threads. {npc} sits you at an old loom beside {him}, and you spend the night weaving a strip of cloud together, too slow, too thick, too crooked, and quite beautiful.

choices.text: Finish the strip and give it to {him}

mem.note: wove me a crooked strip of sunrise

effects.log: The strip is a hand's width of imperfect sunrise. {npc} winds it round a wrist and says it is the best thing {he} owns.

choices.text: Keep the strip and ask {him} to weave the rest

mem.note: asked me to finish the cloth

effects.log: {npc} weaves for a week, and the strip becomes a scarf, and the scarf becomes a promise nobody names.

events.text: A wedding veil of true cloud takes seven years to weave and cannot be made by one person. {npc} asks, with great diffidence, whether you might consider contributing a thread. It is not a proposal. It is, in the language of weavers, entirely a proposal.

choices.text: Give the thread, and a year of your hours

mem.note: wove the veil with me for seven years

effects.log: A year at the loom. The veil is almost done, and you are aware of every stitch as a small sentence in a very long letter.

choices.text: Give the thread, and ask for the veil to be left unfinished

mem.note: left our veil unfinished for later

effects.log: "Unfinished," says {npc}. "For a few more years. Then we shall see." It is the most romantic thing you have ever heard.

events.text: {npc} has woven your scarf into a larger cloth, a banner for the Loom Night, and you stand at the back of the hall as it is unfurled. Your thread runs through it like a gold stitch. "I wanted everyone to see," {he} says. "Even if no one knows what they are seeing."

choices.text: Take {his} hand in front of the hall

mem.note: took my hand under the banner

effects.log: The hall sees. Someone claps. Someone else begins a Loom Night song. {npc} blushes, openly, wonderfully.

choices.text: Whisper that you know exactly what you are seeing

mem.note: whispered that they understood the banner

effects.log: You whisper it. {npc} stops being able to breathe for a moment, then recovers, and takes your arm.

events.text: {npc} is under censure from the Jade Court for a slip in the Rolls that was not theirs, banished from the upper terraces for forty years. You meet {him} on the lower stair, sweeping steps with a bamboo broom, with the unshakeable dignity of someone who has been wronged.

choices.text: Stop and talk to {him}

mem.note: sat with me on the censured stair

effects.log: "Everyone avoids this stair," says {npc}. "You are the first in a month to say hello." You sit on the step and share a flask.

choices.text: Look into the slip in the Rolls

mem.note: went to the Rolls on my behalf

effects.log: You find the clerk at fault, and the file is a mess. It will take a season to unpick, but you start.

events.text: The slip is bigger than it looked: a senior clerk covered it, and now covers the trail. {npc} urges you to leave it, and not risk your standing. "I have my dignity," says {npc}, sweeping. "And my broom." The step is clean. {He} is thinking about you.

choices.text: Press the clerk before the Keeper

mem.note: cleared my name before the Keeper

effects.log: The Keeper hears it with a stiff face. A few months later, the clerk is gone and {npc}'s censure is lifted.

choices.text: Wait out the forty years beside {him}

mem.note: waited out my censure beside me

effects.log: You visit the lower stair every week for decades. The sweepers learn your name. {npc} learns what steadfast looks like.

events.text: The censure is lifted. {npc} walks up the White Stairs in clean robes with a face of studied calm, and meets you at the top. "I do not know how to thank you," {he} says. "So I am going to try several things, in order." The first is a bow. The second is a cup of wine.

choices.text: Accept the thanks and ask for the third

mem.note: thanked me in several things, in order

effects.log: The third is an invitation to dinner, then a second dinner. {npc} says you will be informed of the rest.

choices.text: Ask for nothing, only {his} company

mem.note: wanted nothing from me but company

effects.log: "That one I already had," says {npc}. You ride the next barge together, shoulder to shoulder.

events.text: Forty years later {npc} is restored, and the broom is retired to a hook in your hall. You have grown used to the quiet company of someone whose dignity cannot be touched by a bad decade. They hand you the Court's formal notice of reinstatement and a small stone.

choices.text: Ask what the stone is

mem.note: gave me the stone that steadied them

effects.log: "A spare weight from my broom," says {npc}. "It kept me steady. I want you to have it." You keep it on your desk forever.

choices.text: Offer your own steadiness in return

mem.note: promised to be steady for me

effects.log: You promise to be steady, in whatever fashion needed, for as long as {npc} requires. They accept.

events.text: {npc} was a mortal herbalist from the world below, and eleven years ago they climbed the White Stairs on their own two feet, which almost never happens. Now they live in a rented room above a tea-house, and the other immortals treat them with the fascination one gives a talking dog.

choices.text: Befriend {him} without condescension

mem.note: treated me as an equal in the Isles

effects.log: You introduce yourself with a plain name and no titles. {npc} gives you a look of such grateful surprise that you want to introduce yourself again.

choices.text: Take {him} to the Jade Court and introduce {him} to the right people

mem.note: introduced me to the Court

effects.log: The right people are polite and a little patronising. {npc} survives it with a joke about herbs.

events.text: {npc} still keeps a small herb-garden, the only mortal habit {he} refuses to give up, in a cracked pot on the tea-house roof. One day you find {him} in tears, because the pot is frosting over in the cold air of the isles, and the herb will not grow.

choices.text: Build {him} a warm-glass frame

mem.note: built a frame for my herbs

effects.log: The frame takes you three weekends and a lot of swearing. The herb grows again, and so does something between you.

choices.text: Bring a root-cutting from the world below

mem.note: brought me soil from home

effects.log: You descend, quietly, and return with soil from {his} old village. {npc} presses it to their face and says nothing for a long time.

events.text: {npc} serves you a cup of an herb you have never tasted, grown in the warm-glass frame. It is bitter at first and sweet after. "A mortal cure for homesickness," says {npc}, quietly. "Though what I am homesick for is a person." You wait. {He} looks up.

choices.text: Say you are the person

mem.note: was the person they were homesick for

effects.log: "I rather hoped," says {npc}. The herb-garden blooms a little that evening, as if listening.

choices.text: Ask to hear the whole story first

mem.note: told me their whole story and was heard

effects.log: The story takes three evenings. At the end {npc} says it is a very strange thing to be loved by someone who has listened.

events.text: The village soil sits in a jar on {npc}'s windowsill, and one morning a green sprout pushes through. They call you over to see it. "That village is gone now, a hundred years below," {he} says. "But the soil grew something. Do you think I can, too?"

choices.text: Say you will help them grow

mem.note: let me help them grow

effects.log: You promise to help. {npc} takes your arm, and the sprout leans toward the light as though it, too, had been asked.

choices.text: Say they already have

mem.note: told me I had already grown

effects.log: "Then why am I still afraid?" says {npc}. You stay with them until the question runs out of steam.

events.text: The Jade Court's custom is that a wedding procession is a fleet: a hundred cloud-barges in a line, banners streaming, each carrying a guest. {npc} has asked for a quieter wedding. The Court's Master of Ceremonies has asked for ninety-nine barges, and says nothing about the hundredth.
events.arc: The Wedding of a Hundred Barges

choices.text: Accept the full fleet and be gracious

mem.note: bore a hundred barges for the Court

effects.log: A hundred barges fill the sky. {npc} grips your hand through the whole parade, and smiles at strangers like a saint.

choices.text: Cut the fleet to nine and keep it among friends

mem.note: cut the fleet to nine for my sake

effects.log: Nine barges, nine friends. The Master of Ceremonies sulks for a month. {npc} thanks you with a look that lasts the whole voyage.

events.text: The hundredth barge turns out to carry no guest. It is empty but for a lantern and a note from a distant relative who could not come, and who sends only a wish for the couple's long road. {npc} reads the note and sits down very suddenly on the deck.
events.arc: The Wedding of a Hundred Barges

choices.text: Hold the lantern with {him}

mem.note: held the lantern with me

effects.log: You hold the lantern together as the fleet crosses the clouds. It is the quietest part of the wedding, and the part you remember.

choices.text: Set a cup of wine on the barge for the one who could not come, and send it back

mem.note: sent my absent kin a cup

effects.log: The empty barge drifts home with a cup of wine on its deck. {npc} says that is the kindest thing anyone has done at a wedding.

events.text: At the journey's end the barges moor in a ring round a floating isle, and the Court's herald calls the vow in the Old Tongue. {npc} turns to you, the way one turns to a window, and says the words in plain speech instead, shyly, so only you can hear.
events.arc: The Wedding of a Hundred Barges

choices.text: Answer in plain speech too

mem.note: said our vow in plain words

effects.log: You answer in plain speech. The herald pretends not to notice and calls the vow done. A hundred banners dip at once.

choices.text: Answer in the Old Tongue, with every syllable right

mem.note: learned the Old Tongue for the vow

effects.log: You answer in the Old Tongue with every tone correct. The Court is moved. {npc} is moved more, and says so later, over tea.

events.text: The ninth barge, and the ninth friend, make a toast, and then the second, and the third, until the ring of barges is a ring of laughter. {npc} has taken off the formal crown and put it on your head, and you wear it, crooked, until the sun sets over the isle.
events.arc: The Wedding of a Hundred Barges

choices.text: Wear the crown for the whole feast

mem.note: wore my wedding crown crooked

effects.log: You wear it. The nine friends never let you forget it. It is the best wedding anyone can recall.

choices.text: Return the crown to {him} with a bow

mem.note: bowed to me and gave back the crown

effects.log: You return it. {npc} stares at you, then kisses your hand, absurdly, and the friends howl.

events.text: The wedding feast is planned, and the seating is a minefield. The Eight Houses must each be placed by rank, and each thinks itself first. The Master of the Rolls sends {npc} a diagram that looks like a battle plan. {He} hands it to you with a look of defeat.
events.arc: The Seating of the Eight Houses

choices.text: Seat the Houses by age of lineage

mem.note: rebuilt the seating by rank

effects.log: You seat them by antiquity. The House of the Silent Bell is first, the Vermilion Phoenix last, and that House will remember.

choices.text: Seat them at round tables with no head

mem.note: insisted on round tables for all

effects.log: You order round tables. The Houses mutter; the Master of the Rolls weeps; but no one is placed beneath anyone.

events.text: The feast begins. House Frost Moon and the Clan of the Nine Peaks end up seated face to face, which is an old problem. An elder of one says something about the other's ancestors. {npc} puts a hand on your sleeve: "Do something. Please. Quietly."
events.arc: The Seating of the Eight Houses

choices.text: Propose a toast to both ancestors

mem.note: toasted both feuding houses at our wedding

effects.log: The toast is long and flatters everyone. The elders swallow their insults with the wine.

choices.text: Have the musicians play something so loud nobody can speak

mem.note: drowned a feud in music

effects.log: The musicians oblige with a thunderous reel. Nobody can speak for an hour. By then the elders are dancing.

events.text: At the end of the feast, an old elder of the Jade Lotus House takes you and {npc} aside and gives a blessing in an unexpected form: a pair of plain wooden bowls. "A good marriage is not served in jade," the elder says. "Eat from these when the guests are gone."
events.arc: The Seating of the Eight Houses

choices.text: Thank the elder and eat from the bowls that night

mem.note: ate plain rice with me on our wedding night

effects.log: You eat plain rice from plain bowls, the two of you alone, with the sound of the feast fading. It is perfect.

choices.text: Keep the bowls on the household altar

mem.note: kept the wooden bowls beside the lamp

effects.log: The bowls sit by the lamp for ten centuries. They are used in times of sorrow, and never once chipped.

events.text: The next morning, a note from the House of the Silent Bell: "Thank you. We had not laughed that loudly since the second century." The Master of the Rolls adds a bill for broken furniture. {npc} reads both, and begins to giggle helplessly into a sleeve.
events.arc: The Seating of the Eight Houses

choices.text: Pay the bill with a good grace

mem.note: paid for the dancing at our wedding

effects.log: You pay in spirit stones and a case of plum wine. The Master is mollified, and the House of the Silent Bell sends back a thimble-sized bell.

choices.text: Frame the Silent Bell's note and burn the bill

mem.note: framed the note and burned the bill

effects.log: The note hangs in the hall. The bill goes into the brazier. {npc} says this is how a marriage is run.

events.text: A herald of the Jade Court arrives with a scroll and a lacquer box: the Court's gift for a new household. {npc} and you open it together. Inside, a deed to a small grotto on a distant isle, and a seal granting the right to use the Court's cloud-roads freely.

choices.text: Accept the grotto with thanks

mem.note: accepted the Court's gift with me

effects.log: You accept. The herald bows deeply, with the particular smile of someone who has collected a debt for the Court.

choices.text: Ask what the Court wants in return

mem.note: asked the price of the Court's gift

effects.log: The herald sighs and says nothing, which is itself an answer. {npc} gives you an approving look.

events.text: The grotto is lovely, small, and watched. The cloud-roads carry the Court's clerks, who stop by to "admire the view" with notebooks in their sleeves. {npc} suspects the grotto is bugged with listening-stones. Your tea tastes of surveillance.

choices.text: Find the listening-stones and leave them in place

mem.note: out-bored the Court's listening-stones

effects.log: You find nine. You leave them all, and talk only of tea and weather. The clerks grow bored and stop coming.

choices.text: Return the grotto and keep your own roof

mem.note: gave back the Court's gift to keep our home private

effects.log: You return the deed with a polite letter. The Court is displeased and says so, in the margins of everything you file for a decade.

events.text: A decade on, the Court needs a favour from the household, a small signature on a large treaty. Their clerk reminds you, delicately, of the grotto. {npc} says nothing. The clerk says nothing. The treaty lies between you like a sleeping cat.

choices.text: Sign, and call the grotto even

mem.note: signed the Court's treaty to be rid of it

effects.log: You sign. The treaty is dull and harmless. The Court sends another box of tea, like an apology.

choices.text: Read the whole treaty, aloud, to the clerk

mem.note: read the treaty aloud to the Court's clerk

effects.log: The treaty takes four hours to read aloud. The clerk learns what every clause means. The Court quietly revises seven.

events.text: Because you gave back the grotto, the Court has nothing to hold over the household. A clerk comes to ask a favour and brings a gift instead, at last without a string. {npc} sets the gift on the table and sits across from it, fascinated by the novelty.

choices.text: Accept the gift with no strings and give one back

mem.note: out-gifted the Court

effects.log: The clerk leaves, bewildered. The Court has been out-gifted by a household that wants nothing. It is a quiet revolution.

choices.text: Decline politely and invite the clerk to supper

mem.note: fed a lonely clerk at my table

effects.log: The clerk comes to supper. The clerk, it turns out, is lonely. The clerk comes back a good many times.

events.text: The Vermilion Phoenix House and the Pavilion of Falling Stars have not spoken since the Third Dispute of the Calendar. Both sent your wedding gifts on the same morning. Both are staying on the isle for the feast. {npc} paces the garden and asks you to do something diplomatic.

choices.text: Put them on opposite sides of the isle and ferry the toasts

mem.note: ferried toasts for two feuding houses

effects.log: You run toasts between the two camps all day. You get very good at carrying wine across a garden.

choices.text: Invite both heads to your table for tea

mem.note: sat two feuding heads at my table

effects.log: Tea at one table, cups cooling. The two heads stare at the same plate of cakes and, after a time, one passes it to the other.

events.text: At the feast the two Houses behave, until the dance of the cranes. A young dancer of the Phoenix cuts in on a partner of the Stars, and the whole floor tightens like a drum. {npc} looks at the two dancers, and at the elders, and at you, and mouths a single word: "Now."

choices.text: Step between them and cut in yourself

mem.note: cut in on a feud with a dance

effects.log: You cut in. The dance is awkward and fast. By the end both Houses have forgotten who was insulted.

choices.text: Ask the musicians for the old dance of both Houses

mem.note: found the dance both houses shared

effects.log: The old dance is a joined one, half Phoenix, half Stars. The two heads rise at the same moment, and the floor erupts.

events.text: In the morning the heads of both Houses come to your grotto separately and ask the same question, in the same quiet words: could you stand as the common witness for a reconciliation? {npc} says that is two Houses and one marriage. It is a lot to ask.

choices.text: Agree to witness, for a year

mem.note: witnessed the peace between two Houses

effects.log: A year of witnessing: two Houses, a table, an inkstone. You become the pivot on which an old quarrel turns. It is dull and it works.

choices.text: Decline, and recommend a neutral Elder

mem.note: turned down a hard peace to stay home

effects.log: The neutral Elder does worse, and both Houses blame you in a gentle way. {npc} pats your hand: they will live.

events.text: A year of letters from the two Houses reaches your desk, each accusing the other of sending a wedding gift with a barbed poem hidden in the wrapping. It was the same poem. Someone at the feast, not either House, wrote it. {npc} leans over your shoulder and reads it, and laughs.

choices.text: Find the author and thank them

mem.note: found the poet who split two Houses

effects.log: The author is a junior clerk of the Court who wanted to see what would happen. You thank them. {npc} offers them a better post.

choices.text: Burn the poem and write both Houses the same letter

mem.note: sent two Houses the same peace-letter

effects.log: The same letter to both Houses: the poem is gone, the feud may follow. The Houses, mortified, exchange a wine-gift the next week.

events.text: The old custom of the Isles is the Vow of the Hundred Lamps: on the night of a wedding, a hundred lamps are lit on a terrace, each one for a wish. The last lamp is lit by the couple together. {npc} has been practising the wish for a week, and will not tell you what it is.
events.arc: The Vow of the Hundred Lamps

choices.text: Ask for a hint

mem.note: kept the last wish a secret

effects.log: "No," says {npc}. "It must be a surprise, even to you." You ask no more and spend the week guessing.

choices.text: Offer to share your own wish first

mem.note: told me their wish before the lamps

effects.log: You tell {npc} yours. {He} listens, then says in a small voice that it is nearly the same. Neither of you says the words aloud.

events.text: On the terrace the lamps are lit one by one. At the ninety-ninth a wind comes off the clouds and gutters half of them. A hundred guests watch a hundred small flames shiver. {npc} moves to cup the nearest one, and the whole terrace goes still.
events.arc: The Vow of the Hundred Lamps

choices.text: Cup the lamps together with {him}

mem.note: shielded the lamps with me

effects.log: The two of you, hands round lamps, until the wind eases. Not one flame is lost. The guests exhale as one.

choices.text: Call a barrier from the Isle and still the wind

mem.note: stilled the wind for our lamps

effects.log: A barrier comes up; the wind is shouldered aside. The lamps steady. {npc} says your technique is lovely, and unromantic.

events.text: The last lamp is lit, and the wish read aloud before the Isles: not a grand one. {npc} wishes only that the two of you might see a thousand springs, and bicker through every one of them. The terrace laughs and weeps at once.
events.arc: The Vow of the Hundred Lamps

choices.text: Wish the same, and add a hundred years

mem.note: wished for a thousand springs with me

effects.log: You add a hundred years, as a bonus. The terrace roars its approval. A hundred lamps burn on a hundred-and-one springs.

choices.text: Wish for nothing more than this evening

mem.note: wished for nothing beyond this night

effects.log: You wish for this evening, and it is granted, as modest wishes are. Nobody forgets the wedding of the two who asked for so little.

events.text: Years later, on the anniversary, one lamp is still burning on the terrace, the hundredth, which was meant to go out by dawn. No one has tended it. {npc} stands over it with a cup of tea and the expression of someone who has found a loose thread.
events.arc: The Vow of the Hundred Lamps

choices.text: Leave it burning, and tell no one

mem.note: let our hundredth lamp burn on

effects.log: You tell no one. The lamp burns for a century. Somewhere in it, a wish is still keeping time.

choices.text: Light a new lamp beside it

mem.note: lit new lamps beside the first

effects.log: You light another, and another. The terrace fills, a little at a time, with lamps for wishes kept.

events.text: A Sky Rift opens above the Isle three days before the wedding feast, a tear in the clouds with stars pouring through. The feast is delayed. {npc} watches the rift from the terrace and says, thoughtfully, that it is the most beautiful thing that could have gone wrong.
events.arc: The Wedding Delayed by a Sky Rift

choices.text: Join the Ministries to seal it at once

mem.note: sealed a Sky Rift before our feast

effects.log: You join the Ministries in the sealing. It takes three days. You return, scorched at the sleeves, to a bride or groom who has not once complained.

choices.text: Stay with {npc} and let the Ministries do it

mem.note: stayed rather than sealing the rift

effects.log: You stay. The rift is sealed by strangers. {npc} says you chose well, and means it, and the delay is the best part of the week.

events.text: The rift, it turns out, is not quite sealed. A thin seam of starlight remains above the feast-terrace, humming faintly. The guests, who have waited a week, decide to hold the feast anyway, under the seam, because it is pretty. {npc} peers up at it.
events.arc: The Wedding Delayed by a Sky Rift

choices.text: Hold the feast beneath the starlight

mem.note: held the feast beneath the rift

effects.log: The feast is held under the hum. The wine tastes faintly of star, and no one who drinks it sleeps for two nights.

choices.text: Ask the Ministries to finish the seal first

mem.note: asked them to finish sealing before the feast

effects.log: The Ministries finish. The starlight dies. The feast is grand and ordinary, and {npc} looks at the empty sky a little wistfully.

events.text: The Ministries leave a gift: a thread of starlight preserved in a jar, carried out of the rift as a keepsake. The envoy says it is an old Ministries custom to give such a jar to couples married at a rift. {npc} turns it in the lamplight and it glows blue and cold.
events.arc: The Wedding Delayed by a Sky Rift

choices.text: Keep the jar by your bed

mem.note: kept the rift-starlight by our bed

effects.log: The jar glows at night. It is a quiet, steady light. {npc} falls asleep watching it, and so, soon after, do you.

choices.text: Release it at the next full moon

mem.note: freed the starlight with me

effects.log: You open the jar from the terrace. The thread rises, and joins the stars, and is gone. {npc} takes your hand.

events.text: The starlight seam in the sky has gone quiet. A year after the wedding, you and {npc} look up at the place where the rift was and see the faintest scar: a thin silver line, easy to miss. Children of the isle point at it and say it is where the sky was sewn.
events.arc: The Wedding Delayed by a Sky Rift

choices.text: Tell the children the story of the wedding

mem.note: told the tale of our rift wedding

effects.log: The story grows with the telling. By the time the children are grown, it is a legend. You do not correct it.

choices.text: Keep the scar as a private thing

mem.note: kept our rift scar a private thing

effects.log: You keep the scar to yourselves. A silver line is a good thing to be the only ones to understand.

events.text: It began as a quarrel about the shape of a teacup. Fifty years later, you and {npc} still have not agreed, and the household has taken sides. The tea is served in two cups of two shapes. Nobody dares to say the quarrel is about something else entirely.

choices.text: Propose a truce for one season

mem.note: proposed a truce in the teacup quarrel

effects.log: The truce holds for a season. You sit across from each other with cups of different shapes and talk about nothing at all.

choices.text: Fight on, on principle

mem.note: commissioned a third cup out of spite

effects.log: You fight on. The cups multiply. {npc} commissions a third shape, a spiteful, exquisite masterpiece that holds exactly one sip.

events.text: Seventy years in, the real quarrel finally emerges: {npc} felt overlooked at a banquet in the third decade, and has been quietly furious ever since. You did not know. You thought the cups were the cups. The cups were never the cups.

choices.text: Apologise for a banquet seventy years gone

mem.note: apologised seventy years late

effects.log: You apologise for a banquet you barely recall. {npc} blinks, then laughs until the tears come. "It took you seventy years."

choices.text: Ask what you ought to have done

mem.note: asked what they ought to have done

effects.log: {npc} tells you, point by point, for most of an evening. You listen. It is the best conversation you have had in decades.

events.text: The household is puzzled to find the two cups of different shapes now sit side by side on the same tray. The cook asks whether to unify the set. {npc} and you look at the cups, and at each other. "No," you both say, and the cook retreats.

choices.text: Keep the cups as they are, forever

mem.note: kept the mismatched cups for the next thousand years

effects.log: The cups stay. Every guest asks why, and each of you tells a different, increasingly absurd version of the story.

choices.text: Commission one cup that is both shapes

mem.note: made one cup from our two

effects.log: The potter takes ten years and swears at length. The cup is hideous and perfect, and the two of you drink from it on alternate days.

events.text: A hundred years in, a visitor remarks that the household has never had a real quarrel, and {npc} snorts so hard the tea goes up their nose. You look at each other. The only fights anybody has ever heard of are the ones you had on purpose, because they were fun.

choices.text: Admit it: the quarrel is a hobby

mem.note: turned our quarrel into a game

effects.log: You admit it. The household, appalled and delighted, makes up sides for next time.

choices.text: Declare a ceasefire and plan a proper fight

mem.note: scheduled our next fight with judges

effects.log: You plan the next fight months in advance, with seconds and judges. {npc} wins. You are delighted to lose.

events.text: Your grotto was built for one and has been shared by two for thirty years. The study has two desks, one with a perpetual avalanche of scrolls and one pristine. {npc} proposes, with the diffidence of a person who loves their spouse's mess, a division of the grotto into halves.

choices.text: Accept the division with a line of white chalk

mem.note: drew a chalk line down our grotto

effects.log: A white chalk line down the middle. By morning, the line has been smudged by a sleeve, a cat, and a conspicuous footprint.

choices.text: Refuse and offer to learn their filing system

mem.note: learned my filing system

effects.log: {npc}'s filing system is a masterpiece of private logic. It takes you a year to understand it, and by the end you can't live without it.

events.text: A cloud-storm seeps into the grotto's lower chamber and floods the scroll-room with a foot of fog. Everything is wet. {npc} is wading through the haze, holding a scroll above their head, shouting for you to bring the dry-box. You find it in the wrong half of the grotto.

choices.text: Rescue {his} scrolls first

mem.note: saved my scrolls before their own

effects.log: You save the scrolls and lose half of your own to the damp. {npc} sees it, and does not forget.

choices.text: Rescue your own, then help

mem.note: saved their own scrolls first

effects.log: You save your own first and help after. {npc} is gracious about it. They are wet, and quietly measuring.

events.text: After the flood you and {npc} rebuild the shelves together. This time, the division is by subject, not by owner, and the two desks are pushed together into one long table. The grotto smells of fresh lacquer and old paper. It looks, for the first time, like a shared home.

choices.text: Carve both names above the door

mem.note: carved our names above the door

effects.log: Two names, side by side, in the old script. Visitors stop and read them, and say nothing, and look a little envious.

choices.text: Leave the door unmarked, and the table long

mem.note: kept our house open to all

effects.log: No names. The table is long, the grotto open. {npc} tells guests it is a house for whoever needs one.

events.text: A century passes. The grotto has two desks again: yours is a sprawl of scrolls, and {npc}'s is as neat as a drawn line. Somehow it works. A visitor asks which half belongs to whom. {npc} and you both gesture, simultaneously, at the wrong desk.

choices.text: Laugh and call it a draw

mem.note: liked the mess of my desk

effects.log: You laugh, and the visitor gives up. In the corridor {npc} touches your sleeve: "I like it when you are the mess."

choices.text: Offer to tidy, as a gift

mem.note: attempted to tidy my desk, once

effects.log: {npc} lets you tidy it for a single morning. It takes a day to recover. You never offer again.

events.text: {npc} has been irritable for a month. Last night you heard {him} talking in {his} sleep, quietly, to someone who was not you. At breakfast {he} would not meet your eyes. At noon you found black ash on the cushion where {he} meditates: a heart demon, rising.

choices.text: Sit with {him} through the meditation

mem.note: sat with me through my heart demon

effects.log: You sit opposite and breathe in time. {npc} struggles. By dusk, the ash is thinner and {his} hands are steadier.

choices.text: Call a healer of the Ministries quietly

mem.note: called a healer for my demon

effects.log: The healer arrives and is discreet. The demon is named and weakened, but it is a stranger who helps, not you. {npc} knows.

choices.text: Give {him} space and tend the household

mem.note: gave me space in my darkest week

effects.log: You give space. The house runs quiet and clean. {npc} will remember the silence, in one way or another.

events.text: The demon wears {npc}'s face, and tells {him} things only {he} knows. It whispers that the marriage is a cage, that you cannot possibly understand, that you are only waiting for {him} to fail. {npc} tells you this in a rush, voice thin, and asks: is it true?

choices.text: Say no, plainly, and hold {his} hand

mem.note: said no to my demon and held me

effects.log: "No," you say. "No, no, no." The word becomes a rhythm. The demon flickers, and shrinks.

choices.text: Say it is half true and name which half

mem.note: told me which half was true

effects.log: You name the half that is true: you are sometimes afraid, sometimes tired. The demon, deprived of a lie, is thinner at once.

events.text: The demon is gone, or sleeps. {npc} comes to you at dawn with a cup of tea and a face that has been scrubbed of every defence. "I am not sure it is gone," {he} says. "But I am sure I know what it sounds like, now. And I know your voice is louder."

choices.text: Promise to be louder

mem.note: promised to be louder than my demon

effects.log: "I will always be louder," you say. It is, as promises go, vague and ridiculous, and {npc} laughs wetly and holds on.

choices.text: Offer to learn the sound of it, and help {him} listen

mem.note: learned to hear my demon with me

effects.log: You learn to name the demon's voice from the cadence. Together you build a small habit of noticing.

events.text: Years later, the demon returns in a smaller form, a mutter in the hour before dawn. {npc} knows it for what it is. {He} comes to wake you not in fear but with calm: "It is back. A small one. Will you make tea?" You make tea. The mutter dies in the steam.

choices.text: Make the tea and sit with {him}

mem.note: made tea while my demon muttered

effects.log: The tea is hot, and the dawn comes up grey. The demon is tame, now, a small thing to be tended like a stove.

choices.text: Make the tea and send the household away for the morning

mem.note: cleared the house for my bad morning

effects.log: You clear the house for the morning. It is a luxury and a mercy. {npc} sleeps afterward until noon.

events.text: A traveller climbs the White Stairs, grey-haired, bent, nearly dead of the effort, and asks the gatekeeper for {npc} by a name {he} has not used in three hundred years. They were a mortal when {npc} knew them, a mortal who never forgot. {npc} goes white as paper.
events.arc: A Spouse's Old Flame from Below

choices.text: Go with {npc} to meet them

mem.note: came with me to meet my old flame

effects.log: You walk to the gate together. The traveller sees {npc}, unchanged, and weeps. {npc} takes their hands. You wait a few paces off.

choices.text: Let {npc} go alone, and wait at home

mem.note: let me go alone

effects.log: You let {npc} go. The house is quiet, the tea goes cold. {He} returns after dark, hollow-eyed, and sits beside you without a word.

events.text: The traveller will not live long: the climb has taken too much. {npc} sits at their bedside in a guest room of the grotto and tells them about the three centuries between. You hear it through the wall, in murmurs. Toward evening {npc} comes out and asks, softly, for something.
events.arc: A Spouse's Old Flame from Below

choices.text: Offer the traveller a place in the grotto until the end

mem.note: gave my old flame a place to die

effects.log: You offer, and {npc} thanks you, wordlessly. The guest room becomes a place of quiet vigil.

choices.text: Offer a spirit-stone draught that may add a year

mem.note: bought my old flame a year

effects.log: The draught adds a year. It is not much, but it is something, and {npc} takes it with a hand over their eyes.

events.text: The traveller dies in autumn, peacefully, holding {npc}'s hand. At the small funeral on the isle, {npc} stands apart for a while, then comes and puts an arm round your waist. "Thank you for letting me say goodbye," {he} says. "Even though I did not owe it."
events.arc: A Spouse's Old Flame from Below

choices.text: Say you would have done the same for them

mem.note: said goodbye to my old flame with you beside me

effects.log: "I know," says {npc}. "That is why I married you." They stand together under the funeral cranes.

choices.text: Say nothing, and hold on

mem.note: held me at the funeral without a word

effects.log: You hold on. The autumn wind pulls the funeral cloth taut. {npc} sinks against you, finally, and the quiet is enough.

events.text: {npc} brings you a small casket after the funeral: letters, a pressed cloud-blossom, a comb. "They kept these," {he} says. "Three hundred years. I would like to burn them, but I do not want to do it alone." The brazier is already lit, on the terrace.
events.arc: A Spouse's Old Flame from Below

choices.text: Burn them together, one letter at a time

mem.note: burned my old letters beside you

effects.log: You read none of them aloud, and burn each slowly. By the last letter, {npc} is dry-eyed and calm.

choices.text: Suggest keeping one, as a memory

mem.note: kept one thing from my old flame, with you agreeing

effects.log: You suggest keeping the comb. {npc} considers and nods. It sits on a shelf, a small, polished, quiet thing.

events.text: {npc} announces a seclusion: forty years, behind the Seal of the Inner Grotto, for a breakthrough that cannot be rushed. {He} says it plainly, as one announces the weather. You nod and ask what {he} would like for supper. {He} is quiet, a moment too long.

choices.text: Say you will wait

mem.note: promised to wait through the seclusion

effects.log: "I know," says {npc}. "I would not have asked if I did not." The Seal closes with a hum, and you start counting the days.

choices.text: Ask to join the seclusion

mem.note: asked to join and was turned down

effects.log: "Not this one," {npc} says. "This one is mine." The no is gentle, and the Seal closes. You go home and rearrange the grotto.

events.text: In the twentieth year of {npc}'s seclusion, a stranger comes to the grotto door bearing a gift from a distant House, and a sealed proposal for your hand. They have heard that you are, in effect, alone. They are polite, handsome, and confident of the answer.

choices.text: Refuse and send them off with a cup of tea

mem.note: refused a proposal during my seclusion

effects.log: You refuse the stranger with a cup of tea. They bow and go. You sit all evening by the Seal, and the Seal hums, faintly, as if listening.

choices.text: Ask the stranger to call again in twenty years

mem.note: kept a suitor's card during my seclusion

effects.log: The stranger laughs and goes away. You are not sure what you meant, and you put the card in a drawer to look at later.

events.text: On the fortieth year the Seal opens, and {npc} steps out into the light, a realm higher, with pale tired eyes. {He} looks at the grotto, and the table you have kept laid for forty years, and at you. "You did not move a single cup," {he} says.

choices.text: Say the tea is cold, but the cup is yours

mem.note: kept my cup where I left it for forty years

effects.log: "Warm it," says {npc}. You do. They drink it slowly, standing, in the morning light.

choices.text: Say you moved everything and put it back last night

mem.note: reset the grotto for my return

effects.log: "Thank you for lying," says {npc}, and then, "Thank you for the truth." They have not stopped smiling.

events.text: {npc} steps out of the Seal and finds a card in your drawer. Neither of you speaks for a long moment. {He} reads it, turns it over, and puts it back. "You would have been within your right," {he} says. "I would like to know what you decided."

choices.text: Say you decided to wait, in the end

mem.note: confessed the card and what you decided

effects.log: "Then I am glad you waited," says {npc}. It is not entirely an easy evening, but it is an honest one.

choices.text: Say you did not decide, and that was the wrong answer

mem.note: confessed they had not decided

effects.log: The truth comes out as shaky as a cup. {npc} sits down. Forty years is a long time to be alone, and a short one to forgive.

events.text: A thousand years married, and the Court's herald comes with a scroll of honours for the occasion. {npc} has no use for honours. {He} wants tea. The herald is aghast. The tea is brewed in the kitchen while the herald stands in the hall and reads an increasingly desperate list of titles.

choices.text: Accept the honours politely and pour the tea

mem.note: took the honours but made the tea

effects.log: You accept. The herald weeps with relief. The tea is, as always, the best part of the day.

choices.text: Decline the honours and offer the herald tea

mem.note: turned down honours for tea
